video_title: Can distributed energy work around American utilities?
gist: Nick Chasset, CEO of Octopus Energy US and Uplight, explains why Octopus can only retail in Texas and is instead scaling residential flexibility through Uplight's 85 utility relationships, aiming to lift program participation from 5-20% toward Octopus's ~60%. He argues meter data access and consolidated billing matter more than retail choice, that utility-scale batteries have crushed Texas volatility, that legacy billing systems are the biggest transition bottleneck, and predicts 20-30 GW of connected residential flexibility and falling rates within five years.

themes.theme: Octopus US strategy: routing around utilities via Uplight

insights.claim: Octopus Energy came to the US in 2020 but six years later still sells electricity only in Texas, so it pivoted to selling flexibility services to utilities, supplying residential capacity to aggregators, leasing home batteries for a monthly fee, and (as of September 2026) owning a majority of Uplight.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: US retail-choice barriers forced Octopus into a B2B/utility-enablement model rather than its UK direct-retail playbook.
insights.quote: It came to the US in 2020 intending to do something similar. Six years later, it still sells electricity only in Texas.

insights.claim: Octopus invested in Uplight (announced around March/April 2026) because outside Texas it cannot sell direct to consumers; vertically or partially integrated wires utilities own the billing relationship and are exclusive providers to most US customers, so Octopus chose to work through them.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: The utility, not the retailer, is the gatekeeper for US residential flexibility; vendors selling to utilities capture the channel.
insights.quote: so much of the electric customer experience is run through the wires utility

insights.claim: Uplight runs customer-side programs (home energy reports, flexibility management) for about 85 utilities and says it manages roughly 8.5 GW of flexible load.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Uplight is a scaled incumbent channel into US utilities that Octopus can upsell with its engagement know-how.

insights.claim: The stated test of whether the Uplight strategy is real acceleration rather than a holding pattern is whether utility-run flexibility programs can approach Octopus-level participation (~60%) from today's 5-20%.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Track participation rates at Uplight's flagship utility partners as the key KPI for the thesis.

insights.claim: Octopus plans to prove the model by going deep with a couple of highly motivated utilities (driven by data-center build-out stress or rate pressure) rather than spreading evenly across all 85.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Expect showcase deployments with one or two utilities before broad claims; watch for named case studies.
insights.quote: Octopus has always heavily oriented on the do side of the say-do ratio.

insights.claim: PSEG, New Jersey's biggest utility, is an Uplight customer for home energy reports and flexibility management, and is in active talks to integrate Octopus's customer-engagement know-how.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: PSEG is a likely early proof point for the Octopus-Uplight engagement model in PJM.

insights.claim: Octopus Energy US has doubled its Texas customer base in the last 12 months, from a fairly low base, mostly via standard 6-, 12- and 18-month contracts, and is starting to sell home batteries on a small scale.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Texas retail growth is customer-acquisition now, with flexibility monetization deferred until volatility returns.

insights.claim: Outside Europe and the UK, Octopus has businesses in Italy and Germany each over a million households, fast-growing businesses in Spain and France, and a very fast-growing business in Japan; results similar to the UK follow where markets open access for load.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Octopus's replicable model depends on market design; Japan and continental Europe are growth vectors.

themes.theme: Market design: why the UK works and the US doesn't

insights.claim: The UK has forced choice of supplier, robust markets to monetize flexibility, and half-hourly metering, which together let a retailer like Octopus capture and pass back the full value of customer flexibility.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: These three features are the checklist for which US markets could support Octopus-style retail flexibility.

insights.claim: About 97% of New Jersey residents who have retail choice don't choose and stay with the default provider.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Opt-in retail choice without forced choice yields negligible switching, limiting retail-led flexibility in the Northeast.
insights.quote: something like 97% of residents in the state of New Jersey have a choice, but don't choose.

insights.claim: If he could import one UK feature to the US, it would be meter data access rather than forced retail choice, because many US markets aren't ready for retail competition but data access unlocks customer targeting and settlement through either retailers or utilities.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Meter-data-access policy (not retail deregulation) is the highest-leverage regulatory catalyst for residential flexibility vendors.
insights.quote: I'd say it's the meter data access more so than first choice.

insights.claim: Smart Meter Texas is described as the best-in-class meter data access platform in the US, while getting meter data in PJM is very hard.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Data access asymmetry makes Texas easier and PJM harder for flexibility businesses despite PJM's capacity needs.

insights.claim: In most of the US a residential battery can only monetize coincident demand reduction behind the meter: a home peaking around 2 kW can't realize the export value of a battery that could flex far more, creating a huge mismatch that undermines the battery investment case.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Allowing residential export value to be monetized would materially improve home battery economics.
insights.quote: The average home peaks at 2 kW. You're never going to get the export value of that battery

insights.claim: The single biggest reason Octopus hasn't entered retail-choice states like Pennsylvania is the lack of supplier-consolidated billing: the bill comes from the wires company, the supplier is just a line item, and the customer's first call goes to the utility.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Supplier-consolidated billing reform would be the trigger for Octopus to enter Northeast retail markets.
insights.quote: I'd say the single biggest thing that has held us back to date is consolidated billing.

insights.claim: In states that already have retail-choice frameworks, there are 'no regrets' changes that would enhance consumer protection and make choosing a supplier easier, which would attract companies like Octopus and unlock significant load flexibility.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Watch Northeast retail-choice reform as a potential market-entry signal.

insights.claim: PJM faces a capacity deficit that seems structural and can't be built out of soon because of limited access to turbines and unwillingness to fully count grid batteries as capacity, so demand-side flexibility is needed.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Persistent PJM capacity scarcity supports demand-side and flexibility providers and keeps capacity prices elevated.
insights.quote: they're just not going to be able to build their way out of that capacity deficit anytime soon because of limited access to turbines

insights.claim: Commercial and industrial customers are starting to monetize load flexibility meaningfully, while residential customers are locked out of those benefits; PJM-style structures fundamentally advantage large-load flex over residential flex.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Near-term flexibility revenue accrues to C&I and large-load players; residential upside depends on rule changes.

insights.claim: Because Texas has deployed so much utility-scale solar and storage, price volatility in ERCOT's energy-only market has essentially been destroyed over the last 12-18 months, removing much of the intraday arbitrage value for residential flexibility.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Storage saturation compresses arbitrage spreads; residential flex and merchant battery revenue in Texas face pressure, while consumers benefit from lower prices.
insights.quote: Texas volatility has essentially been destroyed.

insights.claim: The collapse in Texas volatility has hurt Octopus's flexibility business but helped its standard retail business by depressing prices, and Octopus treats the customer relationship as an option to re-engage on flexibility when volatility returns.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Retail customer bases act as call options on future volatility.

insights.claim: The key Texas policy change Octopus wants is letting retailers or residential customers manage transmission and distribution (TDSP) costs through flexibility; residential T&D is billed as flat volumetric, whereas commercial customers above ~50 kW face four-coincident-peak demand charges that make batteries pencil.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: A residential 4CP-style T&D signal in Texas would revive residential battery economics.
insights.quote: So if you're a medium commercial customer, say a 50 kW customer or greater in Texas, you are subjected to your four coincident peak-based demand charge.

themes.theme: Unit economics and future of residential flexibility

insights.claim: The marginal cost of flexibility from devices already in homes (EV charging, routine thermostat pre-cooling) should go toward zero as sign-up friction is eliminated and device API fees are competed away; only perceptible comfort sacrifices and batteries should command payment.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Flexibility from existing devices will commoditize; value shifts to customer ownership and battery assets.
insights.quote: the marginal cost of flexibility for the devices we already have in the home should over time go down to zero.

insights.claim: Hardware makers currently charge flexibility managers API 'gating' fees to access devices like thermostats because there is no single open-source protocol for device access.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Device OEMs collect a toll on flexibility; an open protocol would shift economics to orchestrators and consumers.

insights.claim: In Spain, Octopus installs a 5 kW solar system plus a 10 kWh battery for about 9,000 euros all-in, versus roughly $25,000-30,000 after tax credits in the US.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: US residential solar+storage soft costs are ~3x Europe's; installation cost reduction is the major US lever.
insights.quote: A 5 kW solar system paired with a 10 kWh battery fully installed in the home, 9,000 euros.

insights.claim: Even if flexibility competes energy price spreads away (as in Texas), substantial value remains in deferring transmission and distribution capex by increasing network utilization.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: T&D deferral, not energy arbitrage, is the durable value pool for flexibility providers.
insights.quote: we still have a tremendous amount of transmission and distribution deferral to compete down.

insights.claim: Asked whether flexibility providers put themselves out of business by flattening prices, the guest cites Australia, where mass adoption is now driving rates down, and says Octopus is a customer business that would happily move on if it succeeded.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Flexibility margins are self-eroding; durable moat must come from customer relationships, not spreads.

insights.claim: Dynamic real-time pricing is not necessary for most consumer flexibility value: simple daily shifting from high-cost to low-cost periods captures most benefits and distribution value, with dynamic prices only solving the tail of 5-30 extreme hours a year.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Don't bet on dynamic-tariff rollout as the gating factor; device connection/customer acquisition is the real cost.
insights.quote: I don't actually fundamentally buy into the need for dynamic pricing

themes.theme: Utility program participation and VPP reliability

insights.claim: Typical good US utility demand-response programs see 5-20% participation depending on self-enrollment vs. auto-enrollment, versus about 60% at Octopus.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Large headroom in enrolled capacity if utility programs adopt retailer-grade engagement.
insights.quote: Today a great utility demand response program might see somewhere between 5 to 20% participation rates

insights.claim: Octopus drives participation with simple, clearly quantified offers (e.g., save 25% on EV charging with an overnight flex tariff), one- or two-click device connection, and constant message iteration (e.g., 50 email variants per cohort), whereas utilities send a few mass emails and want to control direct marketing.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Engagement execution, not technology, explains much of the participation gap.
insights.quote: Save 25% on charging your electric vehicle if you sign up for our overnight flex tariff.

insights.claim: Customers with multiple devices currently face separate enrollment journeys per device, causing drop-off on follow-on assets; Octopus is productizing a multi-device version of its app for utilities via Uplight.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: A white-label Octopus app in the utility channel could lift multi-device enrollment.

insights.claim: Target participation: 70-80% of home batteries and essentially every EV should be enrolled in flexibility programs, with 50-60% reasonable for heating and cooling given comfort trade-offs.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Implies large untapped enrolled capacity in existing EV and battery fleets.

insights.claim: A Brattle study commissioned by Uplight found a fully coordinated residential demand stack could raise peak shaving from about 3% to about 5%, largely by moving thermostat participation from ~20% to ~50%.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Near-term peak reduction from existing devices is modest; the bigger value is daily bill savings that make event capacity nearly free.

insights.claim: The 'demand stack' framework: daily load shifting (pre-cooling, managed EV charging) lowers bills every day, which acquires devices at essentially zero marginal cost for the 10-20 event days a year when they are dispatched for peak or feeder constraints.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Bundling everyday savings with event dispatch is the route to cheap scalable capacity.
insights.quote: we've now acquired all these devices at essentially no marginal cost for event-based demand response.

insights.claim: Utility planners don't count enough of Uplight's 8.5 GW as firm, because much legacy enrollment was acquired to meet specific regulatory program obligations rather than distribution or trading operational needs; new enrollments are being designed for operational use.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Expect VPP capacity accreditation to improve as programs shift from compliance to operations.

insights.claim: Uplight reports about 97% accuracy between forecast and actual thermostat dispatch; device-level failures (e.g., Wi-Fi) are handled statistically, unlike a gas plant whose unplanned outage removes all its capacity.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Aggregated DER portfolios can offer reliability comparable to or better than single thermal units.
insights.quote: So, on Uplight, you know, what we find is 97% accuracy

insights.claim: Batteries are a massive unlock for VPPs because their output is metered rather than statistically estimated like thermostats, making providers far more willing to sign service-level agreements for distributed battery fleets.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Metered battery fleets are the path to bankable, SLA-backed residential capacity.
insights.quote: Whereas with the battery it's neither worked or it didn't, can't argue about it. There's a meter.

themes.theme: Kraken vs Uplight and legacy billing

insights.claim: Kraken is most differentiated as an end-to-end stack from billing through flexibility management; integration with billing lets Octopus quickly launch new tariffs and connect them to devices, while utilities on SAP or Oracle may take ~18 months.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Billing system modernization is the precondition for agile rate design and flexibility at scale.
insights.quote: Or, you know, I've heard a story of a utility here in the West Coast that is not able to implement any new rates without deprecating an old one

insights.claim: Legacy utility billing systems are the single greatest hindrance to the energy transition, lower consumer costs, and better customer experiences.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Utility CIS/billing replacement is an underappreciated transition bottleneck and market.
insights.quote: I see these legacy billing systems as the single greatest hindrance to the energy transition

insights.claim: National Grid, which is implementing Kraken's customer solution, should seriously consider replacing its current grid DERMS with Kraken Flex; only one North American utility has announced it runs on Kraken.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: National Grid is a possible Kraken Flex win; Kraken's North American penetration remains very low.

insights.claim: Uplight targets the vast majority of utilities on legacy systems because a flexibility management platform is a far lower bar than replacing a billing system; Octopus will explore blending Kraken Flex components into Uplight.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Uplight and Kraken segment by utility billing modernity rather than directly compete.

insights.claim: Kraken is now separate from Octopus, which retains a small minority stake; widespread Kraken adoption isn't seen as an existential risk to Uplight given the slow pace of utility software decisions, and Uplight could shift toward consumer-facing propositions.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Utility software replacement cycles are long, protecting incumbent DERMS vendors.

themes.theme: Aggregators, data centers and consumer protection

insights.claim: Residential consumers lack adequate protection against platform risks (bricked devices, data misuse), which is why the guest prefers retailer- or utility-led models with obligations to serve over third-party aggregator-led models.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Regulatory scrutiny of residential aggregators is a risk; utility/retailer-aligned vendors may benefit.
insights.quote: I don't think they have adequate protection and I think this is one of the reasons why I'm not generally a huge fan of aggregator led models

insights.claim: Residential flexibility value stacks are often too thin, and aggregators intermediating something consumers don't understand create more potential for rent-seeking than retailer or utility splits governed by competition or regulation.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Thin margins plus intermediation invite consumer-protection backlash against aggregator models.

insights.claim: Data centers' bring-your-own-capacity deals are a valuable route to scale, but PJM-type structures favor large-load flex; behind-the-meter batteries at large commercial sites capture full value without export, unlike homes.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Data-center-driven capacity money flows preferentially to C&I flex.

insights.claim: To win social license amid bill anxiety and community opposition, data centers could partner with utilities and companies like Uplight to fund heavily subsidized batteries, EV chargers and smart thermostats for every customer in a geographic area, e.g., offering $20 off bills.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Data-center-funded community flexibility programs are an emerging channel for residential DER vendors.
insights.quote: If you sign up for Octopus powered by Uplight, you will get $20 off your bill.

insights.claim: Such data-center-funded deals are starting to appear, e.g., Rewiring America signing one with PG&E and Google.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Early precedent for hyperscaler-funded residential flexibility.

insights.claim: Load flexibility could help counter the trend of data centers building behind-the-meter fossil generation such as 200 MW of reciprocating gas engines that raise NOx concerns.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Flexibility competes with on-site gas engines for data-center speed-to-power.

insights.claim: In five years there's no reason 20-30 GW or more of residential flexibility won't be connected, every EV should be connected, and a home battery should be installable all-in for under $5,000.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Implies rapid falls in US residential storage costs and big growth in VPP capacity.
insights.quote: we should be able to in sell and install fully all-in a battery into a household for less than 10 $5,000.

insights.claim: Tesla's announcement that all new Model 3s and Model Ys will have bidirectional charging enabled (with GM making a similar announcement) signals EVs becoming seamless bidirectional home batteries without major electrical upgrades.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: Bidirectional EVs could add millions of home-scale batteries, expanding VPP supply.
insights.quote: Tesla's announcement this last week that go forward all new Model 3s and Model Ys will have bidirectional charging enabled

insights.claim: The guest predicts consumer electricity rates will go down over the next five years as tens of millions of consumers benefit from load flexibility in their homes.
insights.speaker: Nick Chasset (CEO, Octopus Energy US & Uplight)
insights.so_what: A contrarian bullish view on retail rates against the data-center-driven rate-increase narrative.
insights.quote: I think rates are going to go down for consumers in the next 5 years
